narration: The amount you're told you need before you can finally stop working.
You've seen it — about a million and a half dollars.
And almost nobody is anywhere near it.
But here's the scary part. It isn't that people are behind on the number. It's that the number itself quietly stopped working.

heading: Why Most Americans Will Never Retire
narration: So let's do the math. One line at a time.

caption: Three legs. One stool.
narration: Retirement was supposed to stand on three legs. A pension. Social Security. And your own savings.
But two of those legs have quietly been sawn off.

title: Private workers with a pension (%)
narration: In 1980, most workers with a plan had a pension. Today, it's fewer than one in ten.
In its place: a 401k. A pension is a promise. A 401k is a bet.

caption: The government's floor
narration: Then Social Security. The average retired worker collects about nineteen hundred dollars a month.
Call it twenty-three thousand dollars a year. For a lot of people, that's not a floor — it's the whole house.
The four percent rule sets the target. Want forty thousand a year? You need one million dollars.
A million dollars — just to replace one ordinary income.

title: Median retirement savings, by age
narration: And the typical household nearing retirement? About a hundred and eighty-five thousand dollars.
Under the four percent rule, that pays about seven thousand four hundred dollars a year. Six hundred a month.
The math asks a regular person for a million dollars. The typical saver has a fraction of that.
The stool doesn't wobble. It falls.
